Week 2 · HPC · Thursday

Introduction to Holistic Patient Care

Seeing the whole patient in context: physical, psychological, social, environmental, cultural, and spiritual needs
HPC supplemental3 objectivespatient-centered careinterdisciplinary care
ObjectivesThe modelWhat physicians doBenefitsClinical contextRecall

Learning objectives

LO 1. Define the holistic patient care model of care.
LO 2. Recognize the benefits of an HPC model for patients.
LO 3. List the benefits of an HPC model for providers.
One-line anchor
Holistic care means treating the patient as a whole person in context, not reducing them to a diagnosis or a single biologic problem.
01What holistic patient care actually meansLO 1
The lecture defines holistic patient care as approaches and interventions intended to meet a patient's physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual needs. It also emphasizes the patient's social and cultural context, family background, health beliefs, identities, values, and the uniqueness of their needs.
Lecture diagram: the patient sits at the center of four interacting domains - physical/biological, psychological/behavioral, social/environmental, and cultural/spiritual.

Physical / biological

Symptoms, physiology, disease, medications, function, pain, disability, and other biomedical needs.

Psychological / behavioral

Mood, coping, behavior, trauma, adherence, motivation, and other mental-health or behavioral influences.

Social / environmental

Housing, finances, transportation, food, work, family support, insurance, access, and living environment.

Cultural / spiritual

Beliefs, identity, values, culture, language, spirituality, and preferences that shape how care is understood and experienced.

Faculty framing
The domains are interdependent. The point is not to make four separate checklists. The point is to understand how these areas interact to shape the patient's health and treatment plan.
Core assumptions
  • Holistic care is grounded in a humanistic view of the patient.
  • Patients of all backgrounds have the right to receive holistic care.
  • A purely biomedical model is often insufficient to restore health.
  • Ignoring holistic needs can leave important needs unmet and can neglect patient dignity.
02Patient-centered care: the practical version of the modelLO 1
The lecture links HPC with person-centered care: care should respond to the individual's goals, values, and preferences and support effective care planning together.
What this changes for the physician
  • Learn about the patient as a whole person in context, not only the medical problem.
  • Ask nonjudgmentally about the patient's unique views, preferences, and goals.
  • Communicate effectively across cultures, languages, education levels, and developmental levels.
  • Lead and participate in interdisciplinary care.
  • Know when community resources outside the traditional medical model are needed.
  • Include patients and families in decision-making throughout treatment, even when their choices differ from the clinician's preference.
Exam discriminator
Holistic ≠ “alternative medicine.” Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) refers to products and practices outside standard medical care. The lecture explicitly says HPC should not be used interchangeably with CAM.
03Why HPC helps patientsLO 2
Patient-side impact emphasized in the lecture: informed decisions, a care team that knows and listens to the patient, and care aligned with preferences and values.

More informed decisions

Patients are better positioned to understand treatment choices and participate in decisions about their care and well-being.

Continuity + accountability

A coordinated team knows the patient, listens to them, and remains accountable for the overall care plan.

Goals-aligned care

Tools and services are matched to patient preferences and values so care can move toward the patient's own health goals.

Potential health impact

The lecture notes improvements in mental and physical conditions and, in some cases, shorter hospitalization or other markers of recovery.

04Why HPC helps providers and systemsLO 3
Provider/system benefits listed in the lecture.
BenefitWhat the lecture highlights
Patient/family satisfactionImproved satisfaction scores among patients and their families.
Provider reputationEnhanced reputation among health-care consumers.
Staff experienceBetter morale and productivity among clinicians and ancillary staff.
Resource useImproved resource allocation.
System performanceReduced expenses and increased financial margins across the continuum of care.
05What holistic care looks like in real clinical settingsLO 1–3
SettingHolistic / patient-centered behavior
OutpatientFocus on the patient's problem and goals, build a trusted relationship, use empathy and two-way communication, and connect patients to services such as social work, financial counseling, behavioral health, transportation, peer support, or language/literacy resources when relevant.
HospitalRespect the patient's definition of family, involve family in rounding and decisions when desired, provide timely updates, and create environments that support both patient and family needs.
Lecture example: asthma care goes beyond prescribing a rescue inhaler by addressing smoking, living conditions, readiness to quit, and community resources that can reduce environmental triggers.
Reasoning pattern
If a question asks which intervention is most holistic, look for the option that integrates the patient's function, context, preferences, behavioral or social needs, and other members of the care team rather than simply adding another biomedical test or treatment.
Lecture practice-question logic
For the low-back-pain example, referral to physical therapy best represents the holistic approach because it adds interdisciplinary functional assessment and treatment rather than simply escalating imaging, surgery, opioids, or an unrelated medication.
06Closed-note recallall objectives
Try these without looking back:
  1. Name the four major domains surrounding the patient in the HPC model.
  2. Why can the biomedical model alone be insufficient?
  3. What does person-centered care add to the idea of holistic care?
  4. Why is HPC not the same thing as CAM?
  5. List three communication or teamwork expectations for physicians practicing HPC.
  6. List three benefits of HPC for patients.
  7. List three benefits of HPC for providers or systems.
  8. In the asthma example, what makes the plan holistic?
Final synthesis
Whole person + context + communication + shared decisions + interdisciplinary/community resources = holistic patient care.
